items: Recognize all six patterns: Learn to identify timeline distortion, blame inversion, credit theft, outcome reframing, memory denial, and emotional attribution so you can catch them in real-time conversations.
Watch for timeline distortion: Check dates and sequences against your records when you notice conversations shifting about when things actually happened or were said.
Identify blame inversion: Notice whether your valid concerns about problems are being reframed as evidence that you're the source of those problems instead of the person who raised them.
Complete the diagnostic exercise: Write down the last five conversations where you left feeling confused or wrong, and match each one to the specific manipulation pattern used.

Create timestamped records immediately: After any significant conversation with your manager, write down what was said while the details are still fresh and uncontaminated by later reframing attempts.
Build an archive under your control: Keep a personal record of your work contributions, decisions, and achievements that only you can access and no one else can edit or delete.
Log specific language from performance discussions: Capture direct quotes and exact phrases rather than summaries, so you have evidence of what was actually said when memory gets disputed.
Cross-reference your documentation: Before accepting your manager's version of events, compare it against your timestamped notes to identify discrepancies and protect your ground truth.
Regulate your nervous system during destabilizing moments: Use breathing and grounding techniques when you feel off-balance so you're not responding from survival mode during critical interactions.
Distinguish feedback from rewrite campaigns: Check your documented facts against what's being presented to determine if you're receiving legitimate feedback or experiencing reality distortion.
Respond from strategy, not reaction: When pushing back on misrepresentation, use your documentation as the foundation instead of arguing from a destabilized, doubted mental state.
Trust the pattern you noticed: When your nervous system signals that something feels wrong after a conversation, treat that awareness as important data rather than dismissible oversensitivity.
